questions.question: Define tension and compression, name two materials strong in each, and explain the special problem of long thin members in compression.
questions.expected_answer: Tension is a pulling force that tries to lengthen a member; steel, nylon rope and timber along the grain are strong in tension while concrete, brick, stone and glass are weak. Compression is a pushing force that tries to shorten a member; concrete, brick, stone and timber across the grain are strong in compression, as is steel. A long thin member in compression buckles, bowing sideways and collapsing before the material is crushed, so compression members are kept short and thick or are braced along their length.

questions.question: Explain what happens in a beam that carries a load across a gap and use this to explain where reinforcing steel is placed in a concrete slab or step.
questions.expected_answer: The beam bends: the face on the outside of the curve stretches and is in tension, the face on the inside is squeezed in compression, and the neutral axis between them is unstressed. For a simply supported beam loaded in the middle the bottom is in tension; for a cantilever fixed at one end the top near the support is in tension. Concrete is weak in tension, so steel bars or mesh are placed near the tension face, low in a ramp slab or simply supported step and near the top of a cantilevered step at the wall, letting concrete carry compression and steel carry tension. Making the beam deeper also reduces bending.

questions.question: Describe torsion, explain why a hollow tube resists it well, and explain how cross-bracing stops a rectangular frame from racking or twisting, with reference to the handrail.
questions.expected_answer: Torsion is a twisting force about a member's long axis, such as swinging on one end of a long rail. The stress is greatest at the surface and least at the centre, so a hollow tube resists torsion nearly as well as a solid bar of the same diameter at much less weight, which is why rails are tubes. A rectangle of pinned members can rack into a parallelogram without any member changing length, but a diagonal divides it into triangles, which cannot change shape without a side being stretched or compressed, so the push becomes tension or compression in a member. On the handrail, a diagonal or knee brace between post and rail at the ends and landing, with posts set deep, resists the twist from a crowd pushing sideways.
